cards.title: Symptom-Based vs Cause-Based Alerts
cards.teaser: Alert on what users experience, not on what you think is causing it. A server at 95% CPU is a cause; checkout latency above 2 seconds is a symptom. Only symptoms represent real user harm — causes are hypotheses.

runs.text: The Google SRE Workbook draws a foundational distinction between two alert philosophies:

items.text: fire when users are experiencing problems: error rate above SLO, latency above threshold, a critical user journey is failing. They are actionable by definition — if the symptom exists, the user is harmed.

fire when a particular internal resource is misbehaving: CPU high, disk filling, memory pressure. They may or may not correlate with user impact. A disk at 90% is not a user problem until the service stops writing logs or the database crashes.

runs.text: Cause-based alerts have two failure modes: they fire when there is no user impact (false positive → alert fatigue), and they fail to fire for novel failures that bypass the watched cause (false negative → silent outage). A database server can be healthy on all internal metrics while serving stale data due to a replication lag that only manifests as a symptom.
The practical rule from Google SRE:
page on symptoms, ticket on causes

. If a cause is real and persistent, it will eventually manifest as a symptom. Track causes in dashboards and low-urgency tickets so they get resolved before they cause symptoms, but never wake engineers at 3 a.m. for a metric that has not yet hurt anyone.
This maps directly to SLO-driven alerting (Chapter 4): fire when the error budget burn rate is unsustainable. The SLO violation
is
the symptom. Tracing the SLO violation back to a root cause is the on-call engineer's first diagnostic step, not the alert's job.

The Google SRE Workbook's alerting philosophy (Chapter 5) states: "Alerts should be about things that require immediate human action. Everything else is a matter of monitoring." Monitoring informs; alerting demands.
Alert on what the user feels (slow checkout, failed logins, 500s), not on what a machine is doing internally. Internal metrics belong on dashboards; user impact belongs in a page.

cards.title: Page vs Ticket — The Synchronous/Async Split
cards.teaser: A page demands a human awake within minutes. A ticket asks a human to look at something before the next sprint. Conflating the two destroys both: important issues get lost in ticket queues, and unimportant pages destroy sleep.

runs.text: Every alert should be classified as one of three things before it is deployed:

items.text: — requires a human to respond within minutes regardless of time of day. Criteria: user-visible service degradation that will exhaust the error budget within hours; data loss in progress; security breach in progress. Examples: payment service error rate above 5%, login success rate below 95%, SLO burn rate triggering the fast-burn alert.

— requires a human to investigate and fix before the problem becomes a page. Criteria: slow-burn SLO degradation, capacity approaching limits, non-critical service degraded with low traffic impact. Examples: disk at 70% on a log aggregation node, weekly error budget at 40% consumed in first two days.
— a metric worth tracking on a dashboard but not worth any human action. If you cannot state what action the recipient should take, the alert should not fire at all.

runs.text: The test for a page:
would a reasonable engineer, woken at 3 a.m. by this alert, agree it warranted the interruption?
This question, from the Google SRE book, is the most useful calibration tool available. If the answer is no, the alert is misclassified.

Will Larson's writing on on-call hygiene in "Reflective Engineering" emphasizes that the page/ticket split is primarily a social contract: the on-call engineer's implicit agreement is that any page fired is worth their immediate attention. Violating that contract with low-signal pages erodes trust in the entire alerting system.

PagerDuty's 2023 State of Digital Operations report found that 42% of on-call responders received more than 15 pages per week, and of those, the majority rated more than half as not actionable. The page/ticket split is not a best practice — it is damage control.
A page says "fix this right now, user harm is happening." A ticket says "fix this before it becomes a page." If the alert does not map to either of those sentences, it should not exist.

cards.title: Alert Fatigue — When the Signal Drowns in Noise
cards.teaser: Alert fatigue is not a morale problem — it is a systems failure. When the alert-to-action ratio drops below a threshold, engineers stop responding, and the alerting system becomes a liability rather than a safety net.

runs.text: Alert fatigue follows a predictable trajectory:

items.text: Every new service ships with alerts. Thresholds are set conservatively because "better safe than sorry." No alert is ever deleted after the problem it was written for is resolved.
Engineers start acknowledging pages without reading them. Alert emails get filtered to a folder nobody opens. The Slack #alerts channel is muted by 80% of the team.

A real outage fires. The page is indistinguishable from the 50 false-positive pages that fired the same week. Response is slow. The incident takes twice as long to resolve because the on-call engineer had to rediscover that the alert meant something.

runs.text: Measuring alert quality requires tracking these metrics:

items.text: — what fraction of pages result in an engineer taking corrective action? A healthy system targets above 80%. Below 50% is a crisis.
— a rising MTTA is often the first empirical signal of fatigue before engineers themselves report it.
— Google SRE's guidance sets a target of no more than 2 pages per 12-hour shift outside business hours. More than that prevents meaningful sleep and constitutes sustained on-call harm.

runs.text: The remedy is continuous alert review: a standing agenda item at each postmortem to evaluate whether every alert that fired during the incident was correctly classified, and a quarterly audit to delete or downgrade alerts that have not resulted in action in the previous 90 days.

Alert fatigue happens when there are so many alerts that people stop paying attention to any of them — which means the real emergencies get ignored along with the noise. The cure is mercilessly deleting or demoting alerts that do not require action.

cards.title: Runbooks — Documented Response Procedures
cards.teaser: A runbook is the written contract between the alert author and the on-call engineer. It answers: what is this alert saying, what is the blast radius, and what are the first three steps to take at 2 a.m. when you have never seen this before?

runs.text: Every production alert should have a runbook — a document linked directly from the alert body. The link is not optional. An alert without a runbook link implicitly tells the on-call engineer to improvise under pressure in the middle of the night.
A minimal runbook contains:

items.text: — one sentence describing what the alert means in plain language. Not the PromQL expression — a human sentence.
— which users or systems are affected when this alert fires? What is broken? What still works?

— three to five ordered steps an on-call engineer unfamiliar with this service can run immediately. Links to dashboards, diagnostic commands, and example queries. The goal is to characterize the problem within five minutes.
— ranked list of interventions from lowest risk to highest. Start with rollback, then feature flag disable, then traffic shedding, then escalation.
— if the on-call engineer cannot resolve the issue within 30 minutes, who do they wake up? Name the team, the Slack channel, and the secondary pager policy.

runs.text: Runbooks are living documents. The postmortem review after every incident must include a runbook update step: did the existing runbook help? Was it accurate? Was anything missing? An outdated runbook that contains wrong triage steps is worse than no runbook — it wastes time that does not exist during an outage.

In PagerDuty, runbook URLs can be embedded in the alert's custom details field or in the service's escalation policy notes. In Opsgenie, runbooks attach to alert policies. Either way, the URL must be visible in the first notification the on-call engineer receives — not buried three clicks deep.

A runbook is the instruction manual for what to do when an alert fires. It should be detailed enough that a competent engineer who has never touched the service can start triaging the problem within five minutes of receiving the page.

cards.title: On-Call Rotation — Fair, Healthy, Sustainable
cards.teaser: An on-call rotation is a sociotechnical system. If it is fair, engineers accept it. If it is healthy — low page volume, good runbooks, real support — engineers do not dread it. Unsustainable rotations are a leading cause of senior engineer attrition.

runs.text: A rotation design starts with headcount math. Google SRE sets minimum viable rotation depth at 8 engineers for a service with meaningful weekend on-call obligations. Below 8, an individual is on-call too frequently for sustainable on-call to be possible — the rotation loops before engineers have fully recovered.
Key rotation design decisions:

items.text: — one-week shifts are the industry default. Two-week shifts increase the knowledge a person accumulates per rotation but also double the sustained disruption. Shifts shorter than a week create constant handoff overhead without reducing individual burden proportionally.

— every shift change requires a written handoff: open incidents, recent changes, elevated-risk areas, and any tribal knowledge the incoming on-call needs. A 15-minute synchronous handoff meeting is worth more than any amount of ticket grooming.

— holiday, weekend, and overnight shifts must be distributed equitably. "The senior engineers are exempt from weekends" is a policy that creates a permanent underclass of junior engineers doing disproportionate on-call burden.

— no engineer should take primary on-call until they have shadowed at least one full shift and have demonstrated comfort with the runbooks. Throwing a new hire into primary on-call is a reliability risk and an attrition accelerant.

runs.text: Will Larson's "Reflective Engineering" notes that on-call sustainability is a forcing function for reliability work: if the rotation is painful, the team will eventually fix the reliability problems that make it painful — not because they are disciplined, but because they are exhausted. The inverse is also true: a rotation insulated from real consequences (by heroic primary engineers absorbing all incidents) never generates the feedback signal that drives improvement.

A healthy on-call rotation is deep enough that no one is on-call too often, equitable enough that the burden is shared, and well-supported enough with runbooks and tooling that being on-call does not require heroics.

cards.title: Primary, Secondary, and Shadow — Rotation Tiers
cards.teaser: Layered on-call tiers exist to balance coverage, knowledge transfer, and blast radius. Primary handles the page. Secondary backs up the primary. Shadow learns the ropes. Three tiers for three problems.

runs.text: The three-tier model used by Google and widely adopted by large engineering organizations:

items.text: — first responder. Receives all pages immediately. Responsible for triage, incident management, and initial mitigation. Primary does not need to solve every problem alone — they need to characterize the problem, begin mitigation, and decide whether to escalate.

— receives pages if primary does not acknowledge within the escalation window (typically 5 minutes in PagerDuty/Opsgenie). The secondary also serves as a thought partner during complex incidents — a second set of eyes with the same on-call context. On smaller teams, secondary doubles as the escalation path, reducing the need to wake management for incidents the team can handle.

— an engineer new to the rotation who receives all pages but is not expected to respond. They observe the primary's process, ask questions after incidents, read all runbooks invoked, and attend postmortems. Shadow shifts typically last one to two weeks and are a prerequisite for moving to secondary. Shadowing eliminates the dangerous transition from "never on-call" to "primary on-call" with no intermediate stage.

runs.text: PagerDuty implements these tiers through escalation policies: a service's escalation policy chains primary on-call → secondary on-call → team lead → manager, with time-based escalation at each step. Opsgenie uses the same model under "escalation rules" with configurable wait times between tiers.

Not every team needs three tiers. A small team of four engineers with low page volume may sustain primary + secondary only. The shadow tier becomes valuable once the team has regular new-hire or rotation onboarding needs, or when a service is complex enough that primary on-call without prior exposure creates real safety risk.

Primary answers the page. Secondary covers if primary misses it or gets overwhelmed. Shadow watches and learns without being responsible. Three tiers, three different jobs — first response, backup, and apprenticeship.

cards.title: Follow-the-Sun — Geographic 24/7 Coverage
cards.teaser: Follow-the-sun rotations hand on-call responsibility between regional teams as business hours advance around the globe, so no team carries the midnight shift permanently. Coverage becomes a geographic property, not a heroism property.

runs.text: Follow-the-sun (FTS) is a rotation model for organizations with engineering teams spread across multiple time zones. The mechanics: the on-call responsibility transfers from the Americas team at end-of-day to the EMEA team as their workday begins, and from EMEA to APAC as their workday begins. The result is that every team's on-call shift falls within or near their business hours.

FTS solves the fundamental fairness problem of global products: without it, one team — usually the founding team, usually US-based — carries all out-of-hours pages for a service used globally. FTS distributes that burden across geographies.
FTS requirements that teams underestimate:

items.text: — with three geographic shifts, the handoff cadence triples. Every open incident, elevated risk, and in-flight change must be communicated clearly at each transition. Without disciplined handoffs, incidents span multiple shifts with each incoming team starting cold.
— runbooks must be complete enough for any regional team to work the incident. The APAC team cannot page the US team for context at 3 a.m. US time and call it follow-the-sun.

— every team in the rotation needs identical access: same dashboards, same deployment tools, same runbook repository. Regional access controls that block the EMEA team from production systems invalidate the model.
— a follow-the-sun rotation with a two-person team in one region is not sustainable. If one engineer is sick, the other carries the full load. Each regional node needs at least 3-4 engineers.

runs.text: PagerDuty supports FTS schedules natively through time-based schedule layers: you define a schedule restriction per layer that limits when the layer is active (e.g., APAC layer active from 08:00 to 18:00 JST), and PagerDuty automatically routes pages to the active regional schedule.

Follow-the-sun means the on-call baton travels around the globe with the workday — APAC carries it during Asia business hours, EMEA picks it up when they start, Americas takes over when they come online. No team carries the night shift forever.

cards.title: On-Call Compensation
cards.teaser: On-call is work. Acknowledging that with pay, time off, or both is not optional — it is the mechanism by which the organization signals that on-call is a valued, bounded obligation rather than an open-ended expectation that erodes with overuse.

runs.text: On-call compensation models vary by company, country, and employment classification, but the principle is consistent: engineers who carry risk and responsibility outside normal working hours must be compensated differently from those who do not.
The three primary compensation models:

items.text: — a fixed payment per on-call week (or shift), regardless of how many incidents occurred. Common in US tech companies. Typically $200-500/week for junior engineers, higher for senior and staff. Simple to administer and creates predictable cost.

— pay per incident worked outside business hours. Creates the right incentive alignment: teams are motivated to reduce incident volume because high volume translates to high cost (not just engineer pain). Rare in practice because it creates billing complexity.

— on-call engineers who were actively paged and worked incidents outside business hours receive equivalent time off. Google SRE historically used this model: an engineer paged for three hours overnight receives three hours of compensatory time. This model has high employee satisfaction but requires manager discipline to ensure the time is actually taken.

runs.text: Will Larson's writing emphasizes that compensation alone does not make on-call acceptable — the underlying reliability must be improving. A team that receives $500/week to be paged 30 times is not compensated; they are managed into tolerating a broken system. Compensation is a complement to reliability work, not a substitute for it.

In jurisdictions with overtime law (EU, UK, parts of APAC), on-call compensation may have legal minimum requirements separate from employer policy. Legal counsel should review on-call structure in each region.

On-call is real work with real costs — sleep disruption, weekend interruptions, sustained cognitive load. Companies pay for it with cash, with time off, or with both. The payment acknowledges the obligation; the reliability work reduces it.

cards.title: Burnout Signals — Reading the On-Call Health Indicators
cards.teaser: On-call burnout is not sudden — it accumulates through pager volume, sleep disruption, and the creeping sense that the system is ungovernable. The signs are detectable months before an engineer resigns. Most organizations detect them months after.

runs.text: The signals of on-call burnout group into three categories:

items.text: — measurable from incident tooling. Rising MTTA (mean time to acknowledge) indicates that on-call engineers are slower to respond, a leading indicator of disengagement. Rising incident count per shift. Increasing number of incidents escalated past the primary. Increasing number of postmortems with no corrective actions completed.

— observable in team behavior. Engineers begin volunteering for the fewest on-call shifts possible. On-call engineering is described using the phrase "everything is on fire" — the normalization of constant crisis. Postmortems become blame-focused rather than systems-focused. Senior engineers begin discussing leaving the team.

— the most direct harm. Google SRE's operational guidelines specify that an on-call engineer who is paged enough to lose a significant amount of sleep should have their workday protected: no meetings the following morning, reduced commit expectations, recovery time before the next shift.

runs.text: The "everything is on fire" syndrome (sometimes called "alert normalization" or "crisis as background radiation") is particularly dangerous because it is self-concealing: when every shift is high-incident, no single shift is high enough to trigger concern. The aggregate harm accumulates invisibly until an engineer reaches the breaking point.

The structural remedy is a rotating "reliability debt sprint" — a period each quarter where the on-call team addresses only the top 3 sources of pages. No features. No technical debt unrelated to reliability. Over two to three quarters of disciplined reliability sprints, page volume typically drops by 40-60%.

If your on-call rotation has no mechanism to feed alert volume back into the engineering roadmap — no sprint capacity reserved for reliability, no escalation path from "too many pages" to "engineer time to fix" — then burnout is not a risk. It is a scheduled outcome.

Burnout from on-call shows up first in the metrics — slower response times, more escalations — and later in the team dynamics: engineers avoiding on-call shifts, describing their systems as ungovernable. Both are solvable by reducing page volume, which requires engineering time, which requires the organization to treat reliability as work.

cards.title: Alert Routing — Getting the Page to the Right Team
cards.teaser: An alert that reaches the wrong team is worse than no alert at all — it consumes the wrong engineer's sleep, introduces a handoff delay, and is often resolved by "just ping the other team," which is not incident response. Routing is a first-class concern.

runs.text: Alert routing is the logic that maps "this alert fired" to "this team is paged." In small organizations, routing is trivial: one team, one service, one schedule. In organizations with dozens of services and teams, routing becomes a significant design problem.
The major on-call platforms implement routing differently:

items.text: — routing is organized around Services and Escalation Policies. Each service maps to exactly one escalation policy. Routing rules (via Event Orchestration) can inspect alert payload fields and route to different services based on content — e.g., route
to the US SRE team and

— routing is implemented through Teams and Integration routing rules. An incoming alert matches conditions (e.g., alert name contains "database") and routes to the Database team's escalation policy. Opsgenie's routing UI is more visual than PagerDuty's and easier to configure without API access.

— uses routing keys. Monitoring tools post alerts to a webhook URL that includes a routing key. The key maps to an escalation policy in Splunk On-Call. Simple and deterministic; less flexible for content-based routing.

runs.text: Routing quality degrades in proportion to service ownership ambiguity. The most common routing failure mode: a shared service (API gateway, auth, CDN) is owned by no team, so alert ownership defaults to "everyone" which means "no one." Establishing a service ownership registry — even a simple spreadsheet linking service name to on-call team — is a prerequisite for correct routing.

PagerDuty's Service Directory feature provides exactly this ownership registry natively: each service has a team, an escalation policy, and metadata about criticality and business impact. Opsgenie provides equivalent functionality via its CMDB integration.

Alert routing maps a fired alert to the team that owns the service — so the right people wake up, not whoever is unfortunate enough to own the catch-all policy. PagerDuty, Opsgenie, and Splunk On-Call all implement this with slightly different mechanisms but the same goal.

cards.title: Severity Levels — SEV-0 Through SEV-2
cards.teaser: Severity levels exist so that every engineer in the organization — regardless of role — knows at a glance how bad an incident is and what response is expected. Without consistent levels, every incident is treated with ad-hoc urgency, which means the most visible incidents get resources and the quietly bad ones do not.

runs.text: A well-defined severity taxonomy typically uses three to four levels. The most common convention:

items.text: — complete service outage or data loss in progress. All hands. Incident commander assigned. Executive notification within 15 minutes. External status page updated immediately. Example: payment processing completely down, all transactions failing.

— significant user-visible degradation with no immediate workaround. Core user journeys impaired but not completely blocked. Incident commander assigned. Engineering lead notified. Status page updated if customer-facing. Response within minutes. Example: checkout latency above 10 seconds for 40% of requests.

— partial degradation with low user impact or a non-critical service affected. Primary on-call handles alone. No executive notification. No mandatory status page update. Response within the hour. Example: recommendations service returning empty results for 5% of users.
— minor issue with negligible user impact. Tracked as a ticket. No page required. Example: a non-critical internal dashboard returning stale data.

runs.text: The value of severity levels comes entirely from their consistency. If different teams apply different criteria for SEV-1, the severity field communicates nothing. The levels must be defined in a public, canonical document with concrete examples, and teams must be held to the definition during incident reviews.

Severity inflation — the tendency for incidents to be declared higher severity than warranted to attract resources — is a governance problem, not a technical one. Postmortem reviews should track severity accuracy and retroactively correct misclassified incidents.
PagerDuty and Opsgenie both support alert severity fields that map to visual priority levels in the incident timeline. Standardizing your PromQL alert labels (e.g.,
severity="critical"
severity="warning"
) ensures that alert severity flows through to the on-call platform without manual reclassification.

Severity levels are a shared language for "how bad is this right now." SEV-0 means all hands, executives notified, status page live. SEV-2 means the on-call handles it alone, no war room. The levels only work if the whole organization uses the same definitions.

cards.title: Auto-Remediation — From Runbook to Automation Pipeline
cards.teaser: If a runbook says "step 1: restart the pod," that step is automatable. Auto-remediation closes the loop between detection and recovery for well-understood failure modes, eliminating human latency from the most predictable parts of incident response.

runs.text: Auto-remediation is the practice of converting proven runbook steps into automated responses that execute when an alert fires, without requiring a human to wake up, authenticate, and run commands. It is not a replacement for human judgment in novel failures — it is the elimination of human effort for failures that are well-understood and whose remediation is safe to automate.
The auto-remediation pipeline:

items.text: — a monitoring system detects the failure condition and fires an alert with a defined payload.
— the alert payload routes to an automation system (AWS Lambda, Runbook Automation, Ansible Tower, a custom webhook handler) that recognizes the alert type.
— the automation system executes the scripted remediation: restart a pod, scale up a deployment, flush a cache, re-enable a circuit breaker.

— the automation system checks whether the remediation resolved the condition. If resolved: post to the incident Slack channel and close the alert. If not resolved: escalate to the human on-call with context about what was tried.

runs.text: Auto-remediation requires discipline to keep safe. Prerequisites:

items.text: — the remediation action must be safe to run multiple times. Restarting a pod is idempotent; deleting and recreating a database table is not.

— auto-remediation must not trigger in a loop. A restart that resolves a symptom for 10 minutes before it recurs must not restart the service indefinitely. Apply a circuit breaker to the automation itself.
— every automated action must be logged with the alert that triggered it, the action taken, and the outcome. Auto-remediation that is invisible to postmortem analysis creates blind spots.

runs.text: Auto-remediation turns the "restart the pod" step in a runbook into code that runs automatically when the alert fires. You still page a human if the automation fails or if it is a novel problem — but the predictable failures no longer need a human in the loop.

cards.title: Maintenance Windows — Planned Downtime and Alert Suppression
cards.teaser: Maintenance windows are scheduled periods during which alerts are suppressed because the system is intentionally in a degraded state. Without them, planned maintenance generates false-positive pages. With them, on-call engineers know the noise is expected.

runs.text: Every production system requires periodic planned maintenance: database upgrades, certificate rotations, infrastructure migrations, cluster node replacements. During these windows, the system may intentionally exceed alert thresholds — services restart, traffic routes around nodes, latency temporarily increases.

Without maintenance windows, this planned degradation generates real pages to on-call engineers who then spend 10 minutes diagnosing a situation that the team running maintenance already knew about. Multiply this by every planned maintenance event in a quarter and the waste is significant.
Maintenance window implementation across platforms:

items.text: — Maintenance Windows are a native feature. Schedule a window for a service or set of services; all alerts to those services are suppressed for the duration. The window appears in the service timeline so any engineer can see that suppression is active.
— Maintenance schedules suppress alert notifications for specified services during the window. Can be created via the UI, the API, or Terraform for infrastructure-as-code workflows.

— Silences are the equivalent: a time-bounded suppression rule that matches alerts by label set. Silences can be created via the Alertmanager UI or API. They expire automatically and leave an audit trail.

runs.text: Governance requirements for maintenance windows:

items.text: — suppress only the alerts that are expected to fire during maintenance. A "suppress everything" window during a database migration should not also suppress the payment service error rate alert.
— the on-call engineer must know a window is active. Suppression that is invisible to the on-call engineer is indistinguishable from a routing failure.

— a maintenance window that is opened "just in case" for four hours when the work takes 30 minutes leaves a 3.5-hour gap in alert coverage. Open windows for the expected duration plus a 20% buffer, then close them immediately when maintenance completes.

runs.text: Maintenance windows that are left open after the maintenance completes are a reliability anti-pattern. An open window from a maintenance event three weeks ago that nobody closed is a silent SLO hole: your monitoring has been suppressed for weeks and nobody knows.

A maintenance window tells the alerting system: "we know things will look broken for the next two hours because we are intentionally doing work. Do not page anyone." The key rules: scope it to the right alerts, make it visible to the on-call engineer, and close it as soon as the work is done.
